newsitem.title: USA: Exercise cuts breast cancer risks among fit women.
newsitem.headline: Exercise cuts breast cancer risks among fit women.

text.p: Strenuous exercise can dramatically reduce the risk of breast cancer in lean women, a Norwegian study of 25,624 women has concluded.

The study, published in Thursday's New England Journal of Medicine, suggests that exercise may also have a protective effect in average and heavier women, but the link was not statistically significant.
"Physical activity during leisure time and at work is associated with a reduced risk of breast cancer," said the Norwegian team, led by Dr. Inger Thune of the University of Tromso in Tromso, Norway.

In an editorial in the journal, Dr. Anne McTiernan of the Fred Hutchinson Cancer Research Center in Seattle cautioned that "too many questions remain for women and their doctors to make informed decisions on whether, how, and how much to exercise" to prevent breast cancer.

However, there is no question that women -- regardless of their breast cancer risk -- should be exercising. Other studies have already demonstrated that regular exercise cuts the risk of heart disease, stroke, diabetes, obesity, and osteoporosis. It also keeps the mind sharper and lessens the impact of arthritis.
The Thune team used questionnaires and the Cancer Registry of Norway to see which women were getting the most exercise and identify who eventually developed breast cancer.

The researchers adjusted their results for several factors known to increase the risk of breast cancer, including fat intake, how many children they had and how old they were when they became pregnant.
They found that among all women who exercised vigorously and regularly, there was a 37 percent drop in the risk of breast cancer compared to women with a sedentary lifestyle.

But the real beneficiaries of regular exercise turned out to the women who were in the lean category. Regular vigorous exercise cut their risk by a whopping 72 percent. Women with an average or above-average percentage of fat in their bodies were not protected by exercise.
The researchers said genetic influences may be responsible for some of the results, influencing a person's need for physical activity and their predisposition to cancer.
It is also possible that exercise may influence a woman's hormone and metabolic energy balance, both of which may affect the likelihood of developing a breast tumor, the Thune team said.
There was also a decline among women who engaged in moderate exercise, such as regularly spending up to four hours a week walking and bicycling, but the drop was not statistically significant.

Another finding of the study was that women did not have to get their exercise during recreational periods. The women who engaged in heavy manual labor at work had a cancer risk that was 52 percent lower than among women who did not exert themselves at work.
